newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore defends plan for more telcom licences.
newsitem.headline: Singapore defends plan for more telcom licences.

text.p: Singapore Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan said a decision to license additional basic telephone operators from the year 2002 will benefit both the business community and public, the Straits Times said on Monday.

The daily newspaper quoted Mah as telling reporters late on Sunday that the further opening up of the telecommunication market would ensure "Singapore did not shut itself out from the rapid changes and developments in the industry."
On Friday the Telecommunications Authority of Singapore (TAS) said it intended to license additional operators through future tenders to provide commercial services from April 2002.
TAS said this would give successful tenderers involved in a current round of basic service liberalisation sufficient time to stablise their operations and networks.

There are three pre-qualified tenderers in the round for licences to provide basic telecommunications services which closes on December 31, 1997. TAS has said up to two licences will be granted in the round.
Currently only Singapore Telecommunications Ltd has such a license.
The pre-qualifiers in the current round include a consortium comprising Cable & Wireless, Hong Kong Telecommunications, Keppel Telecom and Singapore Press Holdings.
A second consortium comprises British Telecommunications, Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp and Singapore Power and ST Telecommunications.
The third group comprises SembCorp Ltd, Singapore MRT Ltd and WorldCom Inc.
The successful tenderers will be awarded the licences by mid-1998 and will be required to start commercial services from April 1, 2000.

Asked on Sunday if Singapore could sustain more basic telephone operators in addition to those due to get licenses in the current round, Mah said the real issue was not the size of the market but the aim of "keeping Singapore's telecommunications industry at the forefront of global development."

The Straits Times quoted him as dismissing industry criticism that TAS's Friday announcement was sudden and unexpected. He said TAS has always said the government reserved the right to issue more licences.
Mah declined to disclose the number of licences to be awarded.
